electricity: a flow of tiny moving specks called electrons
atom: the tiny building block that all things are made of
electron: a tiny speck inside an atom that can flow as electricity
circuit: a complete loop that electricity flows around
conductor: a material electricity flows through easily, like copper
power station: a large building where electricity is made

Think about how much of your day depends on something you have never once seen. The light you read by. The fan on a hot night. The phone in your hand. The fridge keeping food cool. All of it runs on electricity, a kind of power that flows silently through wires all around you and yet stays completely invisible.

image.note: A home at night, everything lit and running, faint glowing wires shown inside the walls

pages.text: When the power goes off, we suddenly notice how much we lean on it. The room goes dark, the fan stops, screens die. In an instant we are reminded that this quiet, unseen thing does an enormous amount of work for us. So what exactly is it? To find out, we must look at the smallest things there are.

image.note: The same room in darkness, a child holding a torch; the contrast is the point

pages.text: Everything around you, this book, the air, your own hand, is built from tiny pieces far too small to see, called atoms. And inside every atom are even smaller specks, some of which carry a tiny push of their own. A few of these specks, called electrons, can sometimes hop from one atom to the next.

image.note: A simple friendly atom diagram, one small electron circling; labelled clearly

pages.text: Electricity is nothing more than huge numbers of these electrons on the move, all being pushed the same way at once. One electron does almost nothing. But get countless trillions of them flowing together down a wire, and you have enough power to light a city. Electricity is the smallest thing, working in vast crowds.

image.note: A wire shown crowded with tiny electrons all flowing the same direction; a river of specks

pages.text: Electrons will not move on their own. They need a push. That push is given by a battery or by the mains socket in your wall. A battery is like a small store of pushing power, packed and ready. When you connect it up, it shoves the electrons along, and the flow begins.

image.note: A battery with a plus and minus end, arrows showing it pushing electrons out and round; simple

pages.text: Electrons flow easily through some materials and not at all through others. They race through metals, especially copper, which is why nearly every wire has copper inside it. They will not flow through rubber or plastic, which is why wires are wrapped in it. The plastic keeps the power safely on its path, and off your hand.

image.note: A cut wire showing shiny copper inside and plastic coating outside; labelled conductor and insulator

pages.text: Here is the golden rule of electricity: it must travel in a full loop. The electrons flow out from the battery, through the wire, through the bulb, and all the way back to the battery again. This complete loop is called a circuit. If the loop is whole, the bulb lights. Break the loop anywhere, and everything stops.

image.note: A clean circuit: battery, wire, glowing bulb, back to battery; the full loop drawn as an arrow ring

pages.text: This is exactly what a switch does. A switch is just a little gap in the loop that you can open and close. Flick it closed and the loop is complete, so the current flows and the light comes on. Flick it open and the loop is broken, so the flow stops and the light goes out. Now you know what really happens at the wall.

image.note: A switch shown open (gap, bulb dark) and closed (joined, bulb lit); satisfying

pages.text: But where does the electricity in the wall come from in the first place? Most of it is made in huge buildings called power stations. There, something is used to spin a giant magnet inside coils of wire, and that spinning pushes electrons along the wires. Spinning a magnet makes electricity. That is the great secret behind almost all our power.

image.note: A power station with a huge spinning turbine and generator; wires leading out to pylons

pages.text: What does the spinning? It can be rushing water at a dam, or steam from burning fuel, or the wind, or even sunlight caught by special panels. In Nigeria, solar panels on rooftops now catch the strong sun and turn it straight into power. However it is made, it travels down long wires to reach your home.

image.note: Split image: a dam, a wind turbine, and rooftop solar panels on a Nigerian house; all feeding wires

pages.text: Electricity is a wonderful servant, but it must always be treated with respect. The same power that lights a bulb can badly hurt a person if it flows through them. This is why you must never poke anything into a socket, never touch switches with wet hands, and never play with mains wires. Water and electricity together are especially dangerous.

image.note: A clear safety scene: a child stepping back from a socket, an adult nearby; calm, instructive, not scary

pages.text: The safe way to be curious about electricity is with small batteries, bulbs and wires, with a grown-up beside you. A single small battery cannot hurt you, and with it you can build real working circuits and see everything in this book for yourself. Respect the mains. Play safely with the small stuff.

image.note: A child and adult happily building a simple battery-and-bulb circuit on a table; safe curiosity

pages.text: It is hard to imagine now, but not long ago no home had any electricity at all. People lit their nights with fire and lamps, and every machine ran on muscle, animal or water. In only a hundred years or so, electricity changed almost everything about how people live, work and talk to one another.

image.note: A split scene: an old lamplit room; the same room today, bright and full of gadgets

pages.text: So when you next flick a switch, pause for just a second. You are setting countless invisible electrons racing round a loop, pushed all the way from a distant power station, just to make light appear. It is quiet, it is unseen, and it is one of the most powerful tools humans have ever learned to command.

image.note: A child's hand on a light switch, the room lighting up, a faint loop of glowing wire shown; closing
